parts.title: Global Change Is Making Northern Lakes Browner, Lower in Nutrients and Short of Nitrogen, With Different Effects on How Much Tiny Water Plants Grow
parts.abstract:
ABSTRACT

Global change is changing the balance between two things that tiny floating plants in northern lakes need to grow: light and nutrients. This matters for how nutrients and other elements cycle through the lake and for how the whole ecosystem works. We used 29 years (1991–2019) of long-term measurements from 169 natural lakes in Fennoscandia, the region that includes Norway, Sweden and Finland. In these lakes we tracked how four things changed across places and over time. The first was browning, which we measured as total organic carbon (TOC), the carbon in dissolved material that comes from living things. The second was dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN), the simple, non-living forms of nitrogen in the water. The third was total phosphorus (TP). The fourth was the balance between carbon and each nutrient, written as the ratios TOC:TP and DIN:TP.

We then compared these changes with trends that happened at the same time in air temperature, in precipitation (rain and snow), and in nitrogen (N) and sulfur (S) falling from the air onto the land and lakes. This let us see how climate change and the recovery from acid rain together reshape lake chemistry in different parts of the region.

TOC rose in many lakes and DIN fell in most of them. TP trends were mixed. As a result, the ratio of carbon to phosphorus (TOC:TP) rose almost everywhere, and the ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus (DIN:TP) fell. We used mixed linear models, a statistical method that looks for links between measurements while allowing for the fact that we measured the same lakes again and again. These showed that rising TOC was most often linked to falling sulfur deposition and rising precipitation. DIN was generally linked to nitrogen deposition, with temperature and precipitation also playing a part in some subregions.

As browning happened at the same time as DIN:TP fell, lakes became darker. More often than before, their growth was held back by a shortage of both nitrogen and phosphorus together, or by a shortage of nitrogen alone, rather than by a shortage of phosphorus alone. In a group of 74 Swedish lakes, trends in chlorophyll-a (a green pigment we use to measure how much phytoplankton there is) differed from one subregion to another. This shows that the amount of phytoplankton responds in ways that depend on local conditions, not in one uniform way.

Together, these results show that ongoing climate change and lower amounts of material falling from the air are reshaping how carbon and nutrients are linked in northern lakes, and which nutrient holds back growth. This will have consequences for how much new plant material is produced in the future and for how much energy passes up the food chain to animals that eat the plants.

Keywords: browning, carbon–nutrient balance, climate change, dissolved organic carbon, nutrient limitation, recovery from acidification
parts.introduction_first:
Global change is raising the amount of colored dissolved organic matter in many northern lakes. This is material from living things, such as decaying leaves and soil, that has dissolved in the water and gives it a brownish color. Scientists widely call this browning, and it is usually tracked as a rise in dissolved organic carbon (DOC), the carbon in that material (Monteith et al. 2007; de Wit et al. 2016, 2023). Browning is now well documented, and we understand more and more about the main causes behind it. Still, we know little about how browning interacts with two key nutrients, nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P), or about what these linked changes mean for the life in the lakes.

We might expect that more organic matter washing in from the land would bring more total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) into the lakes. Yet several long-term studies of reference lakes, which are lakes with little human impact, report that dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN), the simple, non-living forms of nitrogen in the water, is falling. In some regions, TP is falling too (Canham et al. 2012; Isles et al. 2018, 2023). So DOC, DIN and TP are moving in different directions. This means not only that the amounts of each are changing, but also that the balance between them is shifting, for example the ratios DOC:TP and DIN:TP. These shifts could affect how much phytoplankton (tiny floating plants) grows in the water, and which nutrient holds back that growth (Bergström 2010; Isles et al. 2021; Stetler et al. 2021).
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

Long-term monitoring across Fennoscandia showed a clear shift toward lakes that are browner and lower in nitrogen. TOC rose, DIN fell, and TP changed in mixed ways from region to region. These trends have raised the ratio of carbon to phosphorus (TOC:TP) and, in general, lowered the ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus (DIN:TP). This fits with a move toward growth being held back more often by a shortage of both nitrogen and phosphorus together, or by a shortage of nitrogen alone, as browning gets stronger.

The patterns point to two causes working together to make lakes browner: recovery from acid rain and increasing precipitation. Falling nitrogen deposition (and, in some regions, warming) is lowering the amount of nitrogen in the lakes. Long-term changes in TP, on the other hand, depend more on the region and on the catchment, the land that drains into each lake.

For the life in the lakes, continued rises in TOC are likely to push more lakes toward being held back by a lack of light. At the same time, falling DIN makes it less likely that the extra phosphorus that comes with browning will lead to more phytoplankton. This is especially true where lakes move onto the dark, high-TOC side of the hump-shaped response of phytoplankton to browning. On that side, more browning means less light, so phytoplankton actually grow less.

The balance between carbon and nutrients matters beyond the amount of phytoplankton. It may also change the chemical makeup of the phytoplankton, such as their fatty acids (Lau et al. 2021), and the minerals they contain (Bergström and Karlsson 2019). This in turn affects how much energy passes to zooplankton, the tiny animals that eat the phytoplankton (Elser et al. 2010; Lau et al. 2021; Bergström et al. 2022, 2026).

Our lakes cover a wide range of conditions across the northern forest belt, so these trends are likely relevant beyond Fennoscandia too. This shows the need for continued long-term monitoring that links changes in the air, such as climate and falling material, to lake chemistry and to how living things respond through the seasons.
parts.introduction_rest:
Scientists have noticed browning in northern lakes for decades. At first, they mostly explained it as lakes recovering from sulfur (S) that fell from the air, along with the changes this caused in the catchment and the soil (Monteith et al. 2007; Erlandsson et al. 2008). Sulfur deposition has now dropped to fairly low levels. So browning is more and more often linked to climate and to changes in how water moves through the landscape. Two processes matter here. First, warmer temperatures help forests grow more (Freeman et al. 2001; Finstad et al. 2016; Lucas et al. 2016). Second, more precipitation helps wash dissolved organic carbon (DOC) out of the land and carry it into lakes and rivers (Tranvik and Jansson 2002; de Wit et al. 2016; Imtiazy et al. 2025; Paltsev et al. 2025).

Over the same years, less nitrogen (N) has been falling from the air, and this has changed how the catchment handles nutrients. These changes have been linked to falling DIN in lakes, and in some lakes to falling TP as well (Eimers et al. 2009; Canham et al. 2012; Garmo et al. 2014; Huser et al. 2018; Isles et al. 2018). Browning may partly make up for these nutrient losses, especially for TP. That is because more organic phosphorus, the phosphorus locked inside material from living things, can wash in from the land. However, how strong and how steady this link is seems to differ from region to region and from one period to another (Kortelainen et al. 2006; Isles et al. 2018).

Taken together, differences in climate and in falling material from the air, both between places and over time, can push lakes toward new mixes of DOC, DIN and TP. This changes the balance between carbon and each nutrient, the ratios DOC:TP and DIN:TP. It may also change how much phytoplankton grows and which nutrient holds back that growth (Hessen et al. 2009; Isles et al. 2021; Bergström et al. 2022). Still, we have not tested well enough how consistently changes in the air explain long-term trends in lake chemistry, or whether those links stay the same across places and over time. Often this is because long, well-matched sets of measurements, covering a wide range of conditions, have been hard to find.

Rising DOC can affect phytoplankton in two opposite ways. On one hand, it blocks light, which is bad for the plants. On the other hand, material from the land may bring more nutrients, which is good for them (Kelly et al. 2018; Bergström and Karlsson 2019; Vasconcelos et al. 2019; Isles et al. 2021). Because these two effects pull in opposite directions, phytoplankton often show a hump-shaped response to DOC. When DOC is low, more of it means more phytoplankton. Once DOC gets high enough that a lack of light takes over, more DOC means fewer phytoplankton (Thrane et al. 2014; Kelly et al. 2018; Bergström and Karlsson 2019). In real lakes, this turning point often comes at around 10–12 milligrams of DOC per liter of water (Solomon et al. 2015; Bergström and Karlsson 2019). The exact value may vary, though, depending on the features of each lake.

How phytoplankton respond also depends on the balance between the nutrients they are given, especially the ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus (DIN:TP). This ratio decides which nutrient holds back their growth (Bergström 2010; Elser et al. 2009; Isles et al. 2020). For example, suppose DIN:TP falls and growth shifts from being held back by a shortage of phosphorus to being held back by a shortage of nitrogen, even though DOC does not change much. This could mean less phytoplankton, because less nitrogen is reaching the lakes as less nitrogen falls from the air (Bergström and Jansson 2006; Elser et al. 2009; Bergström et al. 2022). These ideas suggest that browning and changing nutrients should lead to different phytoplankton responses in different places. Those places differ in their catchments, their climate and their history of sulfur and nitrogen deposition (Hessen 2013; Isles et al. 2021; Johnson et al. 2025).

Even though we expect this, many studies of how DOC, nutrients and phytoplankton are linked rely on surveys that cover only a short time or only a few places. Such surveys may miss long-term trends in DOC, DIN, TP and the balance between them (Isles et al. 2021; Stetler et al. 2021; Paltsev et al. 2024). As a result, few studies have looked across many places and many years. Such studies would link changes in the air to water chemistry over several decades, and then connect those changes to how much phytoplankton grows and which nutrient holds back its growth.

Long-term monitoring programs in Fennoscandia give us a rare chance to fill these gaps. They run for decades and include lakes that differ widely in DOC, in nutrients, in climate and in falling material from the air (Isles et al. 2018, 2021; Paltsev et al. 2024). Here, we use 29 years of data (1991–2019) from 169 lakes. We measure long-term trends in browning, in DIN and in TP. For browning we use total organic carbon (TOC) as a stand-in for DOC. We also look at how the balance between carbon and each nutrient (TOC:TP) and the balance of nutrients reaching the phytoplankton (DIN:TP) changed at the same time.

The color of organic matter matters for how much light reaches the phytoplankton. To capture this, we also look at how strongly the organic matter absorbs visible light, using a measure called Abs420:TOC. It is the amount of light absorbed at a wavelength of 420 nanometers, divided by TOC. We then compare these trends in water chemistry with trends in key changes in the air: air temperature, precipitation, and sulfur and nitrogen deposition. Finally, we use chlorophyll-a (Chl-a), a green pigment, from a smaller group of Swedish lakes as a stand-in for how much phytoplankton there is. With it, we check whether the changes in water chemistry match changes in the amount of phytoplankton. We also check whether shifts in DIN:TP suggest that lakes are moving from one nutrient shortage to another.

In particular, we ask:
parts.methods:
2.

Materials and Methods

2.1.

Weather Data

We took estimates of air temperature and precipitation (rain and snow) from the TerraClimate dataset (Abatzoglou et al. 2018). This dataset divides the land into a grid of squares, each about 4 km across (1° of latitude by 24° of longitude). For every square it gives monthly values, filled in between weather stations so that the map is complete. For each lake and each year from 1991 to 2019, we worked out two yearly averages. The first was the average of the highest air temperature of each day over the year, which we call mean annual maximum air temperature (MAT, in °C). The second was the average precipitation over the year (MAP, in mm). To see how things changed over the long run, we also averaged MAT and MAP over 5 years at a time for each lake, once for 1991–1995 and once for 2015–2019.

2.2.

Material Falling from the Air

We downloaded estimates of material falling from the air from the European Monitoring and Evaluation Programme (EMEP). These estimates are also laid out on a grid and filled in between measuring sites. We received them as NetCDF files, a common format for storing large sets of data, for each calendar year from 1991 to 2019 (Colette et al. 2016; Amann et al. 2018). For each lake and each year, we took the values from the grid square that held the lake's monitoring site.

We then added up the different forms of each element. For nitrogen, we added the wet deposition of ammonium (NH4+) to the wet deposition of all nitrogen oxides (NOx total). Nitrogen oxides are gases such as nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide. We call this yearly total nitrogen deposition (Ndep). For sulfur, we added the wet deposition of sulfur dioxide (SO2) to the wet deposition of sulfate (SO4−2). We call this yearly total sulfur deposition (Sdep). For each lake, we also averaged Ndep and Sdep over 5 years, once for the first 5 years (1991–1995) and once for the last 5 years (2015–2019).

2.3.

Lake Measurements, Choosing Lakes, and Making the Data Match

We gathered long-term measurements of lake water chemistry from national monitoring programs in Norway, Sweden and Finland. We focused on lakes in the northern forest belt whose catchments were fairly untouched, with little direct human disturbance. The countries sampled their lakes in different ways. In Norway, 78 lakes were sampled once a year in autumn (late September to early November). In Finland, 26 lakes were sampled 4–6 times a year, and in Sweden, 97 lakes were sampled 4–6 times a year.

To make the data match, we used only autumn samples from the surface layer of the water. This gave us one value per lake per year for 1991–2019, a total of 29 years. Not every lake was sampled in every year, so some years were missing. Missing data can distort trends over time, so we kept only lakes that were missing 15% or fewer of their yearly values over the whole study period.

This left us with 169 lakes. In Norway there were 75 lakes, with a median area of 0.52 km² and an average of 0.79 ± 0.70 km². (The median is the middle value when all lakes are lined up from smallest to largest. The number after ± is the standard deviation, which shows how widely the values spread around the average.) In Finland there were 19 lakes, with a median area of 0.31 km² and an average of 0.53 ± 0.59 km². In Sweden there were 75 lakes, with a median area of 0.53 km² and an average of 1.15 ± 1.90 km².

These lakes cover a large area, and the regions differ a lot in climate, in how much material has fallen from the air over the years, and in their catchments. Some of these differences even change in opposite directions over time in different regions. If we had pooled all the lakes together, we would have hidden these important regional causes, trends and responses. So instead, we sorted the lakes into nine subregions (Figure 1), grouping lakes that were similar in climate, in material falling from the air, and in the plants and animals that live there. We followed the reasoning of de Wit et al. (2023). This gave us the following regions: Norway southwest (24 lakes), Norway southeast (13), Norway north (38), Sweden southwest (30), Sweden southeast (15), Sweden northwest (15), Sweden northeast (15), Finland south (10) and Finland north (9).

In the past, southern Fennoscandia has received the most sulfur and nitrogen falling from the air. Meanwhile, TOC and TP usually rise from west to east, from low levels in Norway to higher levels in Finland (Henriksen et al. 1998).

FIGURE 1

The subregions of Fennoscandia in our study.

All chemical measurements were made in accredited laboratories, which are officially approved to meet quality standards. The laboratories followed international (ISO) or European (EN) standards. In Norway, the work was done by the Norwegian Institute for Water Research (Skjelkvåle et al. 2001). In Finland, it was done by the Finnish Environmental Administration (1991–2015) and by Eurofins Environment Testing Finland (2016–2019) (Vuorenmaa et al. 2014). In Sweden, it was done by the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences (Fölster et al. 2014). This matches earlier studies that combined data from many lakes (Fölster et al. 2014; Vuorenmaa et al. 2014; de Wit et al. 2023).

We calculated dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) as ammonium (NH4+) plus nitrate (NO3−). We used TOC as a stand-in for dissolved organic carbon (DOC), because more than 90% of the TOC in Finnish and Swedish lakes is dissolved (Köhler et al. 2002; Kortelainen et al. 2006). For Swedish lakes, we also had a measurement of how much light the water absorbed at a wavelength of 420 nm, taken in a 5-cm cuvette (a small container used in the instrument). We call this Abs420, measured in m−1. We used it to work out how strongly the organic matter absorbs visible light for its amount of carbon, written as Abs420:TOC (Abs420 [m−1]/TOC [mg L−1]) (Eklöf et al. 2021; Isles et al. 2021).

We calculated three ratios. The first was DIN:TP, the ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus, counted by number of atoms (a molar ratio). The second was TOC:TP, the ratio of carbon to phosphorus, counted by weight (TOC [μg L−1]/TP [μg L−1]). The third was Abs420:TOC. Before the analysis, we converted DIN:TP, TOC:TP and Abs420:TOC to a logarithmic scale (base 10). On this scale, each step of 1 means the ratio is ten times larger or smaller. We write all of these converted values as log, for example log DIN:TP (Isles 2020; Isles et al. 2021).

In Norway, ammonium and TP were not measured in some lakes, or were measured only now and then in the early years. So for each Norwegian lake, we calculated the average ammonium and TP for 2002–2019. We used these averages to fill in missing ammonium values. We also used them to fill in TP for the first 5 years (1991–1995) and for the few missing years after that. We used these filled-in values to build DIN and the ratios when we compared the two periods. However, when we looked at TP trends in Norwegian lakes, we used only years with measured TP (see Section 2.4).

Across Norwegian lakes, ammonium made up a smaller share of DIN than nitrate did. Across all lakes and years, ammonium was on average 29% of DIN, with a median of 23%. The coefficient of variation, which shows how much this share varied from lake to lake and year to year, was 76%. TP levels were generally low. As a result, changes in the Norwegian DIN:TP ratio came mainly from changes in nitrate.

2.4.

Trends in Weather and in Lake Water Chemistry

For each lake, we tested whether MAT, MAP, Ndep and Sdep showed a monotonic trend, meaning a steady rise or a steady fall over time. We used Mann–Kendall tests for this (Kendall 1975). This test checks whether values tend to go up or down over time, even if they do not change at a constant rate. We also estimated how fast each value changed per year, using Sen's slope (Sen 1968). Sen's slope is the median of the slopes between every pair of years, so a few unusual years do not throw it off.

To sum up each subregion, we averaged the Sen's slopes of all its lakes, including both positive and negative slopes. We then tested whether each subregion's average slope was different from zero, using a one-sample t-test. This test checks whether the average of a set of values differs from a chosen number, here zero. We used a significance level of α = 0.05, which means we called a trend statistically significant when a slope this far from zero would turn up less than 5% of the time if there were really no trend. We also report results at α = 0.10, so that our results can be compared with earlier studies (Bergström et al. 2024; Paltsev et al. 2024). Finally, we averaged the subregion averages to describe the overall trends across Fennoscandia.

To measure long-term changes in water chemistry and in the balance between carbon and nutrients, we calculated 5-year averages for each lake for 1991–1995 and for 2015–2019. We did this for TOC, DIN, TP, log DIN:TP, log TOC:TP and log Abs420:TOC. We then expressed the change as a relative difference between the two periods. To test whether a value differed between the two periods, we used paired t-tests, which compare the same lakes in both periods. When the data did not meet the conditions a t-test needs, we used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests instead, which do a similar job without those conditions.

We also wanted to know whether the links between TOC and the nutrients, or between TOC and how dark the water was, had changed over time. For each lake, we fitted a straight line through its 5-year averages of TP, log DIN:TP, log TOC:TP and log Abs420:TOC against TOC, separately for the two periods (1991–1995 and 2015–2019). We then used ANCOVA, a test that checks whether the slopes of such lines differ between groups, to test whether the slopes differed between the periods.

Besides comparing the two periods, we calculated Mann–Kendall trends and Sen's slopes for each lake for TOC, DIN, TP, log DIN:TP, log TOC:TP and log Abs420:TOC. Because Norwegian TP data were mostly missing before 2002, we calculated TP trends for Norway for 2002–2019. For all other water chemistry measurements, and for all other countries, we used 1991–2019. As before, we summed up each subregion by averaging the Sen's slopes of its lakes, including both positive and negative slopes. We then tested whether each subregion's average slope was different from zero, using a one-sample t-test (α = 0.05) and reporting results at α = 0.10.

2.5.

How Weather and Material Falling from the Air Affected Lake Water Chemistry

We looked at how differences in weather and in material falling from the air, across places and over time, affected lake water chemistry within each subregion. For this we used mixed linear models. For each lake and each year, the weather and deposition measurements were MAT, MAP, Ndep and Sdep. The water chemistry measurements were TOC, DIN, TP, log DIN:TP and log TOC:TP.

In these models, the weather and deposition measurements were fixed effects, meaning the factors whose links to lake chemistry we wanted to measure. Lake identity was a random intercept, meaning each lake could have its own starting level. This allowed for the fact that we measured the same lakes again and again over the years. Most of the measurements followed a roughly bell-shaped (normal) pattern, but not all. So we converted MAP, Ndep, Sdep, TOC, DIN and TP to a logarithmic scale to make them closer to bell-shaped. The ratios were already on a logarithmic scale, as log DIN:TP and log TOC:TP. MAT was already close to bell-shaped, so we did not convert it.

We ran many tests, and when you run many tests, some will look significant just by chance. To guard against this, we applied the Holm–Bonferroni correction to the p-values of all the mixed linear models that looked at water chemistry. This correction makes the bar for calling a result significant stricter.

2.6.

How Trends in Water Chemistry Affected Trends in Chlorophyll-a

Detailed measurements of chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) were available only for the Swedish monitoring lakes (74 lakes), from 1996 onward. Our water chemistry data were mostly from autumn. To match the two, we used only autumn measurements of chlorophyll-a, from 1996 to 2019 (24 years). For each lake, we tested whether chlorophyll-a showed a steady rise or fall over time using Mann–Kendall tests, and estimated how fast it changed per year using Sen's slope.

Earlier studies have shown that the amount of phytoplankton may not change in a straight line as lakes brown. Instead, it may follow a hump-shaped response, rising at first and then falling (Bergström and Karlsson 2019; Isles et al. 2021). This happens because browning comes with changes in how many nutrients are available and in the balance between carbon and nutrients. However, our goal was not to find one single link between chlorophyll-a and TOC for all of Fennoscandia. Instead, we asked whether lakes whose water chemistry and carbon–nutrient balance changed more over time also showed stronger steady rises or falls in chlorophyll-a. We thought this was the better approach. Each subregion covers only a small part of the full range of TOC, so it cannot capture the whole hump-shaped response seen across northern lakes.

So, within each Swedish subregion, we used mixed linear models to see how the Sen's slopes of chlorophyll-a were linked to the Sen's slopes of TOC, DIN, TP, log DIN:TP and log TOC:TP. We found two lakes, Stor-Arasjön in northwest Sweden and Fagertärn in southeast Sweden, that did not fit the pattern of the others. We spotted them using histograms and quantile plots of the residuals, which are the leftover differences between what a model predicts and what was actually measured. We left these two lakes out of the subregion analyses they belonged to. As before, we adjusted the p-values of all the chlorophyll-a mixed linear models with the Holm–Bonferroni correction.

2.7.

Shifts in Which Nutrient Holds Back Growth Across Fennoscandia

Lakes can be held back by a shortage of phosphorus alone, by a shortage of both nitrogen and phosphorus together, or by a shortage of nitrogen alone. To see whether lakes moved between these states, we compared the spread of each lake's 5-year average DIN:TP (on a logarithmic scale) and TOC between 1991–1995 and 2015–2019 across Fennoscandia. For Swedish lakes, we also looked at how chlorophyll-a and its trends changed between the first 5 years of the chlorophyll-a record (1996–2000) and the last 5 years (2015–2019). We defined the nutrient shortage categories using published cut-off values (Bergström 2010; Isles et al. 2018). A lake was held back by a shortage of phosphorus alone when log DIN:TP was above 0.9. It was held back by a shortage of both nitrogen and phosphorus together when log DIN:TP was between 0.5 and 0.9. It was held back by a shortage of nitrogen alone when log DIN:TP was below 0.5.

2.8.

Software

We ran the Mann–Kendall tests in R (version 4.2.2; R Core Team 2022), using the trend package. We fitted the mixed linear models in JMP Pro (version 15.0.0). We did the other analyses in SigmaPlot (version 14.0).
parts.discussion:
4.

Discussion

4.1.

How the Air Shapes Browning and Nutrient Trends

Most lakes in Fennoscandia are becoming browner and lower in nutrients. TOC is rising, DIN is falling, and in some regions TP is falling too. These shifts have raised the ratio of carbon to phosphorus (TOC:TP) and, in general, lowered the ratio of nitrogen to phosphorus (DIN:TP). This links the chemical changes in the lakes to large-scale forces in the air: temperature, precipitation, and falling nitrogen (N) and sulfur (S).

Overall, as browning gets stronger and DIN:TP falls, lakes are moving toward being held back by a shortage of both nitrogen and phosphorus together, or by a shortage of nitrogen alone. The amount of phytoplankton responds in ways that differ from region to region.

Browning (TOC) trends were similar across Fennoscandia, except in northwestern Sweden, and they were mainly linked to falling sulfur deposition. TOC rose most in areas that were once acidified, which is every subregion except northwestern Sweden and northern Finland. This supports the idea that lakes are still recovering from acid rain as sulfur deposition falls (Monteith et al. 2007; Erlandsson et al. 2008; Räike et al. 2024).

In many subregions, rising precipitation happened at the same time as rising TOC. This fits with wetter conditions carrying more organic matter from the land into lakes (Freeman et al. 2001; Erlandsson et al. 2008; de Wit et al. 2016; Imtiazy et al. 2025). TOC, by contrast, was only weakly linked to temperature and nitrogen deposition. This suggests that warming, which can make plants on land take up more carbon, and changes in how land is used played a smaller part in TOC over the 29 years we studied (Finstad et al. 2016; Räike et al. 2024).

TP trends varied more from subregion to subregion. TP fell in most places in northern Fennoscandia. In the southern subregions, however, browning seemed to soften the fall in TP, which agrees with earlier studies (Kortelainen et al. 2006; Huser et al. 2018; Isles et al. 2018; Nilsson et al. 2024). TP trends were mainly linked to nitrogen deposition. This fits with the land around lakes holding on to more phosphorus as lakes recover from acid rain (Huser et al. 2018). Other features of the air were only weakly related to TP, and in Finland TP trends were not linked to any of them.

Warming can also make the land around lakes greener, and this can help the land hold on to more phosphorus, especially in mountain landscapes. That means less phosphorus reaches clear-water lakes with little dissolved organic carbon (Goedkoop et al. 2025). In line with this, TP fell mainly in subregions whose lakes had little TOC (northern Finland, northwestern Sweden and northern Norway). This suggests that the growth of plants on land is an important cause (Goedkoop et al. 2025). What drives long-term falls in TP is likely to differ from region to region and from catchment to catchment (Stetler et al. 2021; Isles et al. 2023).

Even though TP changed in different ways, TOC:TP rose steadily across Fennoscandia. It was linked mainly to sulfur deposition and, to a lesser degree, to precipitation. This supports what has also been reported for lakes in the United States: more carbon for each unit of phosphorus, and carbon and phosphorus changing out of step with each other over time (Stetler et al. 2021).

DIN fell almost everywhere, and the fall was strongest in southern Norway. These trends followed falling nitrogen deposition. This fits with less nitrogen falling straight onto lake surfaces (Isles et al. 2018), and/or less DIN being carried in from the land (Bergström et al. 2008; Hessen 2013). In Norway, DIN also fell as precipitation rose, which fits with the extra water diluting the nitrogen (Hessen et al. 2009).

DIN was lower where temperatures were higher, especially in northern Finland. This fits with the land holding on to more nitrogen as the land turns greener and forests grow more (Hessen et al. 2009; Lucas et al. 2016; Goedkoop et al. 2025). Lower DIN may also reflect more denitrification, a process in which microbes turn nitrogen into a gas that escapes into the air, which can happen more when TOC is higher (Weyhenmeyer and Jeppesen 2009). Continued warming, rising precipitation and falling nitrogen deposition therefore suggest that DIN in lakes will keep being pushed downward.

Because TP trends varied, DIN:TP trends were less even than DIN trends. Still, falling DIN:TP clearly won out: 123 trends were negative and only 35 were positive. This produced statistically significant declines in Norway, southeastern Sweden and northern Finland. A trend is called statistically significant when, if there were really no trend, a pattern this strong would rarely appear by chance alone. Falling DIN:TP was mainly related to falling acid deposition from the air and to rising precipitation.

4.2.

From Lake Chemistry to What Holds Back Growth: Changes Are Expected, but Not the Same Everywhere

TOC rose, DIN fell, and DIN:TP generally fell. Together, these changes show that across Fennoscandia, phytoplankton are shifting toward being held back more often by a shortage of both nitrogen and phosphorus together, or by a shortage of nitrogen alone. How much phytoplankton grows, and in which direction, should vary. This is because the amount of phytoplankton depends both on how brown a lake is and on which nutrient holds back its growth, as shown by DIN:TP (Bergström et al. 2022).

To picture this, imagine a hump-shaped response curve. As a lake gets browner, phytoplankton first grow more, because more nutrients arrive. But once TOC passes a certain level, the water blocks so much light that phytoplankton grow less. Seen this way, browning can boost phytoplankton in fairly clear lakes by bringing in more nutrients. In browner lakes, where a lack of light is the main problem, browning can hold them back. These outcomes should differ between regions, because TOC and DIN:TP vary from place to place and change over time in different ways (Kelly et al. 2018; Bergström and Karlsson 2019; Isles et al. 2021). As a result, the effects on how carbon and nutrients pass along the open-water food chain may differ from region to region (Bergström et al. 2026).

TOC:TP rose between 1991–1995 and 2015–2019. Even so, lakes with more TOC still tended to have more TP, so the two stayed linked across places. This means browning still tends to raise TP, but more slowly in 2015–2019 than in 1991–1995. We also looked at how strongly the water absorbs light at a wavelength of 420 nanometers (Abs420), which tells us how much colored organic matter is in the water. In Swedish lakes, the ratio of this light absorption to TOC did not change between the two periods. This suggests that long-term changes in light are driven by changes in how much TOC there is, rather than by changes in the kind of organic matter.

4.3.

How Phytoplankton Responded in Different Parts of Sweden, and What This Means for Fennoscandia

Trends in the amount of phytoplankton, measured as chlorophyll-a, were mixed across Sweden. They also differed in how they were linked to changes in water chemistry, including TOC and DIN:TP. The strongest rises and falls were in southern Sweden. There, browning was steady and DIN fell, but DIN:TP changed little, because browning partly softened the fall in TP.

In the southwest, these lakes therefore stayed mainly held back by a shortage of phosphorus (DIN:TP = 1.0). In the southeast, they moved toward being held back by a shortage of both nitrogen and phosphorus together (DIN:TP = 0.9). In both cases there was still enough DIN for phytoplankton to grow if browning and TP inputs continued.

In southwestern Sweden, chlorophyll-a trends were mainly negative where TOC trends were negative, and also negative, but more weakly, where DIN:TP trends were negative. This pattern fits the hump-shaped response curve. Below a certain TOC level, browning and the TP that comes with it can help phytoplankton grow more. Above 10–12 mg L−1 (milligrams per liter), though, a lack of light takes over and phytoplankton grow less.

Southwestern Sweden was also the only subregion where average chlorophyll-a was significantly lower in 2015–2019 than in 1996–2000, and where the average trend was negative. This fits with browning pushing many lakes onto the dark, high-TOC side of the response curve. The negative link between chlorophyll-a and DIN:TP also fits with these lakes being held back mainly by a shortage of phosphorus.

In southeastern Sweden, chlorophyll-a trends were mainly positive where TP trends were positive. Lakes here were less brown and became browner more slowly than in the southwest. This left more of them in clear water, where rising TP can help phytoplankton grow when DIN:TP is fairly high. Average chlorophyll-a did not change between 1996–2000 and 2015–2019, and average trends were close to zero. This fits with some lakes rising and others falling.

In northern Sweden, lakes are more often held back by a shortage of nitrogen alone, or of both nitrogen and phosphorus together, and their DIN:TP is lower overall (Isles et al. 2020; Bergström et al. 2008, 2022). Browning was strongest in the northeast, where TOC is higher. In the northwest, browning was weaker and less steady, and DIN and TP fell in lakes with less TOC (see also Johnson et al. 2025). Chlorophyll-a trends were weaker than in southern Sweden, as we would expect with lower DIN:TP.

In northwestern Sweden, chlorophyll-a was mainly negative where TP trends were negative, and also positive, but more weakly, where DIN:TP trends were positive. This fits with the responses we would expect in phytoplankton when they are held back by a shortage of nitrogen (Bergström et al. 2022). Average chlorophyll-a trends were slightly negative. In northeastern Sweden, chlorophyll-a trends were positive where TP trends were positive. This fits with browning helping phytoplankton grow somewhat, but the effect is likely weaker than in the south because less DIN is available. Average trends were slightly positive. In both northern subregions of Sweden, average chlorophyll-a rose slightly between 1996–2000 and 2015–2019, but these increases were not statistically significant.

Finally, Swedish lakes range from very clear, nutrient-poor mountain lakes to dark, brown forest lakes. The same range of conditions also appears in Norway and Finland. So the patterns we found in Sweden's subregions give a reasonable basis for what to expect across Fennoscandia.

In Norway, phytoplankton may grow more as browning continues. This is because Norwegian lakes are still mostly held back by a shortage of phosphorus (DIN:TP > 0.9) and have not yet become extremely brown or dark (TOC < 12 mg L−1). Browning has been strongest in southeastern Norway, so phytoplankton there are likely to have grown the most, along with the TP that came with it. In Finland, phytoplankton are also likely to grow more as lakes become browner, especially in southern Finland, where DIN:TP is higher.

4.4.

Limitations

Our study covers a long time and many lakes, but it still has some limitations. First, we could only study phytoplankton in Swedish lakes with long-term chlorophyll-a records. So what we say about Norway and Finland should be treated as well-informed expectations, not as direct evidence.

Second, we worked out chlorophyll-a trends from autumn samples. These may miss the summer peak, and they may differ from trends based on summer samples, which helps explain why different studies find trends of different strength. Even so, our autumn trends broadly agree with those of Paltsev et al. (2024), who used average chlorophyll-a from summer (June–September), and of Johnson et al. (2025), who counted phytoplankton cells in August. Both studies also show different paths for phytoplankton in southern and northern Sweden. In the south, some lakes rose and others fell, while in the north most lakes rose. This difference between places has been linked to differences in which kinds of phytoplankton live in each region and in local conditions (Paltsev et al. 2024; Johnson et al. 2025).

Finally, the air measurements describe large-scale forces, but they do not describe the catchments. Features such as changes in plants, soils and the paths water takes over the land likely shape how each region responds, especially for TP. Continued long-term monitoring that links falling material and climate to the features of the land around lakes, and that measures living things through the seasons, will be essential. It will help us work out what causes phosphorus to change, and make better predictions as lakes keep becoming browner and their nutrients keep shifting.

3.

Results

3.1.

How Air Temperature, Precipitation and Falling Material Changed Across Fennoscandia

We split Fennoscandia into subregions, which are smaller areas within each country (see Figure 1). We then compared the first five years of our study (1991–1995) with the last five years (2015–2019).

The average yearly maximum air temperature (MAT) and the average yearly precipitation (MAP) both rose across Fennoscandia. The rise was larger in the south than in the north (Figure 2; Table 1). When we looked at all the years together, temperature went up in every subregion, which shows that warming was widespread (Table 1). Precipitation was more mixed. Some lakes showed a fall and others a rise (Table 1). Even so, average yearly precipitation went up in every subregion except northwestern Sweden, and it rose most in southern Norway (Table 1; Figure 2).

Nitrogen deposition (Ndep) and sulfur deposition (Sdep) fell sharply between 1991–1995 and 2015–2019. Today, large parts of Fennoscandia receive little acidic material from the air (Figure 2). The highest present-day nitrogen deposition is found in southern Norway and southern Sweden. The highest present-day sulfur deposition is found only in southern Sweden (Figure 2). Across lakes, and in the averages for each subregion, both nitrogen and sulfur deposition went down. The steepest falls were in the southern subregions (Table 1).

3.2.

How Lake Water Chemistry Differed Between 1991–1995 and 2015–2019

Lake water chemistry changed significantly across Fennoscandia between 1991–1995 and 2015–2019 (Figure 3). To describe the typical lake, we use the median, the middle value when all lakes are lined up from lowest to highest.

TOC rose (p < 0.001), from a median of 4.2 to 5.9 mg L−1 (milligrams per liter). DIN fell (p < 0.001), from 44 to 29 μg L−1 (micrograms per liter, or thousandths of a milligram). TP, by contrast, did not change significantly between the two periods (p = 0.19), with medians of 7.2 and 4.9 μg L−1. A result that is not significant means we could not show a change. It does not prove that there was none.

The median TP did not move significantly, but the spread of TP values did narrow. Fewer lakes had very low TP (below 2.5 μg L−1, or log TP below 0.4) or high TP (above 10 μg L−1, or log TP above 1) in 2015–2019 than in 1991–1995 (Figure 3). Here log means the logarithm, a scale on which each step up means ten times more.

FIGURE 3

Histograms showing how the average values of Fennoscandian lakes were spread out in the first five years (1991–1995, blue) and the last five years (2015–2019, light orange) of the study. The measurements are log TOC (mg L−1), log DIN (μg L−1), log TP (μg L−1), log TOC:TP (carbon-to-phosphorus ratio, by weight), log DIN:TP (nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio, by number of atoms) and log Abs420:TOC (a measure of how much light the water absorbs at a wavelength of 420 nanometers, compared with its TOC). Bars where the two periods overlap are shown in brown.

The ratios between carbon and nutrients shifted in step with these changes in amounts. The carbon-to-phosphorus ratio (TOC:TP) rose, from 2.81 to 2.97 (p < 0.001). The nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio (DIN:TP) fell, from 1.04 to 0.81 (p < 0.001). The third ratio, Abs420:TOC, which we used only for Sweden, did not change significantly (from 0.17 to 0.22, p = 0.37) (Figure 3).

In both periods, lakes with more TOC also tended to have more TP. In other words, TOC and TP were strongly positively correlated. However, the link between them was significantly different in the two periods (p = 0.014). The line linking TOC and TP was steeper in 1991–1995 than in 2015–2019 (Figure 4a), which shows that the pattern of TOC and TP across the lakes changed over time.

In the same way, the carbon-to-phosphorus ratio rose as TOC rose in both periods, but the slope of this line was different (p = 0.014). In 2015–2019, each unit of TOC came with a higher carbon-to-phosphorus ratio (Figure 4b). The nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio fell as TOC rose in both periods, but the slopes did not differ (p = 0.367) (Figure 4c). This shows that the link between TOC and the nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio across the lakes stayed stable, even though in the most recent period, 2015–2019, lakes moved toward higher TOC and lower DIN:TP.

The plots show how water chemistry changed between the first five years (1991–1995, blue) and the last five years (2015–2019, light orange) of the study. Each value is the average for that period. We calculated p with a method called analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), which compares the slopes of two lines.

3.3.

Long-Term Trends in Water Chemistry in Each Subregion

We also looked at long-term trends, using all 29 years, and these differed from subregion to subregion (Figure 5; Table 2). TOC rose in every subregion except northwestern Sweden. Across all lakes, 153 showed rising trends and only 7 showed falling trends. The strongest rises in TOC were in southeastern and southwestern Sweden and in southeastern Norway, where TOC went up by more than 0.1 mg L−1 per year, or about 3 mg L−1 over 29 years.

The amount of phytoplankton, measured as chlorophyll-a (Chl-a; μg L−1 per year), is also shown. TP trends varied more from subregion to subregion (Table 2; Figure 5). Across all lakes, 48 showed falling trends and 32 showed rising trends. TP fell steadily in northern Fennoscandia, with average slopes from −0.011 to −0.053 μg L−1 per year, or −0.3 to −1.5 μg L−1 over 29 years. In southeastern Sweden, by contrast, TP rose significantly (0.049 μg L−1 per year), at the same time as TOC was rising (Table 2).

DIN generally fell in every subregion. The falls were especially strong in southern Sweden and Norway, with slopes from −0.552 to −3.441 μg L−1 per year, or −16 to −100 μg L−1 over 29 years (Table 2; Figure 5). Across Fennoscandia as a whole, TOC rose significantly and DIN fell significantly (Table 2).

The trends in the ratios between carbon and nutrients all pointed in the same direction. The nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio fell in most lakes: 123 showed falling trends and only 35 showed rising ones. The steepest falls were in Norway, with average slopes from −0.008 to −0.012 per year, or −0.2 to −0.35 over 29 years. The ratio also fell in northern Finland (−0.008 per year, or about −0.2) and in southeastern Sweden (−0.003 per year, or about −0.09).

The carbon-to-phosphorus ratio rose in every subregion, with average slopes of 0.006 to 0.013 per year, or 0.174 to 0.377 over 29 years. The largest average rise was in northwestern Sweden (Table 2; Figure 5). Across Fennoscandia as a whole, the carbon-to-phosphorus ratio rose significantly (Table 2).

Even with these trends, the lakes still differed a great deal from place to place (Figure 6). TOC and TP generally rose as you move from Norway toward northeastern Fennoscandia, toward Finland. DIN was higher in southern Fennoscandia, with the highest amounts in southwestern Norway. The carbon-to-phosphorus ratio was lowest in southwestern Norway and rose toward the northeast. The nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio was highest in Norway and fell eastward toward Sweden and Finland (Figure 6).

Chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) is shown only for the Swedish subregions. Values are averages from the last five years (2015–2019) of the study.

3.4.

How Air Temperature, Precipitation and Falling Material Were Linked to Lake Water Chemistry Across Places and Time

Our mixed linear models found several significant links between the measurements in the air and lake water chemistry within subregions (Figure 7; Table S1). In many models, the random lake effect was significant. This part of the model allows for the fact that each lake may respond in its own way, and it showed that lakes within the same subregion responded differently to the air measurements (Tables S1 and S2).

FIGURE 7

Heatmap of the results of the mixed linear models for the 1991–2019 records of lake water chemistry and of the air measurements (temperature, precipitation, nitrogen deposition and sulfur deposition) in each Fennoscandian subregion. Colors show whether each air measurement had a positive or negative effect on water chemistry, based on the size of the estimated effect (see Table S1 for details). Green = positive effect, blue = negative effect, white = not significant (p ≥ 0.05). The closer the color is to white, the weaker the effect.

In most subregions, rising TOC (browning) went together with falling sulfur deposition and rising precipitation (Figure 7). Nitrogen deposition was linked to higher TOC in southern Norway and northern Finland. For TP, nitrogen deposition had positive effects in five of nine subregions, which means lakes had less TP where less nitrogen fell from the air. In northern Norway and southwestern Sweden, TP was also lower where precipitation was higher. The patterns for the carbon-to-phosphorus ratio mostly matched those for TOC: it was generally lower where sulfur deposition was higher and higher where precipitation was higher (Figure 7; Tables S1 and S2).

The links between DIN and the air measurements varied more from subregion to subregion. As we expected, DIN was higher where more nitrogen fell from the air in many subregions. In southern Sweden, northern Finland, and northern and southwestern Norway, DIN was also lower where temperatures were higher. In Norway, DIN was lower where precipitation was higher, while in southwestern Sweden it was higher where precipitation was higher (Figure 7; Tables S1 and S2). Because DIN was more consistently linked to the air measurements than TP was, the nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio often showed the same links as DIN.

3.5.

How Water Chemistry Was Linked to Chlorophyll-a Trends (Sweden)

Across the Swedish subregions (1996–2019), chlorophyll-a rose in some lakes and fell in others (Figure 5). The strongest changes were in southern Sweden. In southwestern Sweden (29 lakes), 19 lakes showed falling trends and 10 showed rising trends. In southeastern Sweden (15 lakes), 5 lakes showed falling trends and 7 showed rising trends. In northern Sweden, the trends were generally weaker but still mixed. In northeastern Sweden (15 lakes), 5 showed falling and 6 rising trends. In northwestern Sweden (15 lakes), 4 showed falling and 5 rising trends.

We also compared average chlorophyll-a in 1996–2000 with 2015–2019. In most subregions, the average changed only a little. It rose slightly in northwestern Sweden (from 1.8 to 1.9 μg L−1) and in northeastern Sweden (from 3.1 to 3.3 μg L−1), and stayed about the same in southeastern Sweden (4.2 μg L−1). The exception was southwestern Sweden, where the average fell from 4.6 to 3.9 μg L−1. There, chlorophyll-a in 2015–2019 was significantly lower than in 1996–2000 (paired t-test, p = 0.041). A paired t-test compares the same lakes in two periods.

The mixed linear models showed that, in southeastern Sweden, lakes whose TP rose faster also tended to have chlorophyll-a that rose faster (Table 3). In southwestern Sweden, lakes whose TOC rose faster tended to have chlorophyll-a that rose more slowly, while lakes whose carbon-to-phosphorus ratio rose faster tended to have chlorophyll-a that rose faster (Table 3). In this subregion, chlorophyll-a also tended to rise faster where DIN rose faster, and more slowly where the nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio rose faster (p < 0.1; p = 0.066–0.070). In northeastern and northwestern Sweden, the links between TP trends and chlorophyll-a trends were weaker (p < 0.1; p = 0.054–0.085). In northwestern Sweden, the nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio tended to rise faster where chlorophyll-a rose faster (p = 0.09).

3.6.

How the Nutrient That Holds Back Growth Changed Across Fennoscandia

To judge which nutrient was holding back phytoplankton growth, we used the balance between carbon and nutrients. We tracked how TOC and the nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio changed between two five-year periods (1991–1995 and 2015–2019), both across Fennoscandia and within each subregion (Figures 8 and S1; Tables 2 and 4). Overall, lakes moved toward higher TOC and toward being held back more often by a shortage of nitrogen alone, or by a shortage of both nitrogen and phosphorus together (Figure 8).

FIGURE 8

The contours show where the lakes cluster: (a) 100% (light grey), 67% (grey) and 33% (dark grey) of the lakes, and (b) 100% (light red), 67% (red) and 33% (dark red) of the lakes. The horizontal dashed lines mark the nitrogen-to-phosphorus levels for each nutrient that holds back growth: above 0.9 for phosphorus alone, 0.5–0.9 for nitrogen and phosphorus together, and below 0.5 for nitrogen alone (Bergström 2010; Isles et al. 2018).

We used a TOC level of 12 mg L−1 to sort lakes into clear and brown. In 1991–1995, 155 lakes were below this level and 14 were above it. In 2015–2019, 146 lakes were below it and 23 were above it. The average TOC was 4 mg L−1 in the clear group and 14 mg L−1 in the brown group in 1991–1995, and 5 mg L−1 and 15 mg L−1 in 2015–2019.

As the nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio fell, the number of lakes we classified as held back by nitrogen alone (below 0.5) rose from 7 to 12. The number held back by nitrogen and phosphorus together (0.5–0.9) rose from 49 to 59. The number held back by phosphorus alone (above 0.9) fell from 113 to 98 between 1991–1995 and 2015–2019 (Figure 8). This shows an overall shift toward more lakes that may be held back by nitrogen, or by nitrogen and phosphorus together.

However, the trends were not the same in every subregion (Figures 5, 8 and S1; Tables 2 and 4). Apart from northwestern Sweden, the subregion averages show browning across the regions, with the strongest rises in TOC in southern Sweden and southeastern Norway (Table 4; Figure S1). Over the same period, the average nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio fell in Finland and Norway, stayed about the same in southern Sweden and rose in northern Sweden.

These shifts in the ratio suggest that, in some cases, the nutrient holding back growth changed. Northern Finland moved from being held back by nitrogen and phosphorus together toward possibly being held back by nitrogen alone (0.6 to 0.5). Southern Finland moved from being held back by phosphorus alone toward possibly being held back by nitrogen and phosphorus together (1.1 to 0.9). Northern Sweden stayed held back by nitrogen alone or by nitrogen and phosphorus together, even though its ratio rose slightly (the inferred boundary is 0.6–0.8). Southeastern Sweden stayed near the boundary between possibly being held back by phosphorus alone and by nitrogen and phosphorus together (about 0.9).

In contrast, southwestern Sweden and Norway stayed possibly held back by phosphorus alone (inferred boundary above 0.9), even though the Norwegian lakes had a lower nitrogen-to-phosphorus ratio in 2015–2019 than in 1991–1995 (Table 4).
